nodes.title: Ghana Empire
nodes.short: A major West African state whose wealth was tied to trans-Saharan exchange.
nodes.description: The Ghana Empire, also called Wagadu in Soninke traditions, developed in the western Sahel. Its rulers controlled access to gold-producing regions and taxed commerce moving across the Sahara. It was not the same state as the modern country of Ghana.

nodes.title: Mali Empire
nodes.short: A powerful West African empire associated with Mansa Musa, trade and centres of learning.
nodes.description: The Mali Empire emerged in the western Sahel in the thirteenth century. Its rulers drew wealth from agriculture, trade and gold. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–25 attracted wide attention, while Timbuktu and other cities developed as centres of scholarship and commerce.

nodes.title: Songhai Empire
nodes.short: A West African empire that grew around the Niger bend and trans-Saharan trading cities.
nodes.description: Songhai became a major power in the western Sahel during the fifteenth century. Under rulers including Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad, it controlled commercial routes and cities such as Gao and Timbuktu. Its imperial power was broken by a Moroccan invasion in 1591.

nodes.title: Great Zimbabwe
nodes.short: A monumental stone-built city and political centre of the Shona-speaking peoples of southern Africa.
nodes.description: Great Zimbabwe developed between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries and became a major political and trading centre. Its dry-stone architecture and imported objects provide archaeological evidence of regional and long-distance connections. The site is central to Shona history and was built by local African communities.

nodes.title: Kingdom of Aksum
nodes.short: A Red Sea kingdom connecting northeast Africa with Arabia and the Mediterranean world.
nodes.description: Aksum grew in the northern Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands and became a major power linking Africa, Arabia and the Greco-Roman world. Monumental stelae, royal inscriptions and coinage provide evidence of state organisation and exchange. Christianity became established at Aksum in the fourth century.

nodes.title: Kingdom of Benin
nodes.short: An Edo kingdom renowned for court art, bronze casting and political institutions.
nodes.description: The Kingdom of Benin developed in the forest region of present-day southern Nigeria. Its court supported specialised guilds and highly skilled artists, including brass casters. Benin's history is documented through oral histories, material culture and written records; British forces invaded the kingdom in 1897.

nodes.title: Qin Dynasty
nodes.short: The dynasty that unified several Chinese states and established imperial institutions.
nodes.description: The Qin state unified rival kingdoms in 221 BCE under Qin Shi Huang. The dynasty standardised important systems of administration, writing, weights and measures, while large state projects included frontier walls and the emperor's mausoleum complex. Qin rule ended in 206 BCE, but its imperial model shaped later Chinese history.

nodes.title: Han Dynasty
nodes.short: A formative Chinese imperial dynasty known for state institutions, trade and cultural development.
nodes.description: The Han dynasty consolidated and extended the imperial state established by the Qin. Its long history included expansion of overland connections later grouped under the name Silk Roads, growth of bureaucratic institutions and major developments in material culture. Han legacies became important reference points for later Chinese dynasties.

nodes.title: Tang Dynasty
nodes.short: A cosmopolitan Chinese empire marked by cultural flourishing and Eurasian connections.
nodes.description: Tang China became a major power of the medieval world. Its capital Chang'an drew merchants, clerics and envoys from across Asia, while diplomacy and trade connected the empire to wider Eurasian networks. The period is associated with achievements in poetry, painting, sculpture and civil service examinations.

nodes.title: Heian Period
nodes.short: A period of Japanese court culture associated with classical literature, poetry and refined arts.
nodes.description: The Heian period began when the imperial capital moved to Heian-kyo, present-day Kyoto, in 794. Court society fostered distinctive literary and artistic traditions, including works by women writers such as Murasaki Shikibu. Chinese institutions and cultural forms were adapted into a distinctive Japanese court culture.

nodes.title: Edo Period
nodes.short: A long era of Tokugawa rule that saw political consolidation and vibrant urban culture.
nodes.description: Under the Tokugawa shogunate, Japan experienced more than two centuries of relative internal peace. Urban centres expanded, commercial networks grew, and popular arts such as kabuki and ukiyo-e flourished. The period was not one of complete isolation: controlled diplomatic, commercial and intellectual exchanges continued.

nodes.title: Meiji Restoration
nodes.short: The political transformation that restored imperial rule and accelerated Japan's modern state-building.
nodes.description: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and established a new government in the emperor's name. Meiji leaders centralised administration, reorganised military and education systems, and pursued rapid industrial and institutional change. These reforms transformed Japan's international position and generated major social changes.

nodes.title: Achaemenid Empire
nodes.short: A vast Persian empire whose administration connected the Mediterranean to Central Asia.
nodes.description: Founded under Cyrus the Great, the Achaemenid Empire became one of the largest states of the ancient world. Its rulers governed diverse peoples through regional administrative structures and roads. Persepolis, founded by Darius I, served as a ceremonial and political centre whose architecture expressed imperial authority and cultural exchange.

nodes.title: Sasanian Empire
nodes.short: A major Iranian empire that shaped politics, religion and culture across late antiquity.
nodes.description: The Sasanian Empire ruled Iran and neighbouring regions from 224 to 651 CE. It was a major rival and diplomatic counterpart of the Roman and later Byzantine empires, and its institutions and artistic traditions influenced neighbouring societies. Its conquest by Arab Muslim armies in the seventh century transformed West Asia.

nodes.title: Abbasid Caliphate
nodes.short: A caliphate whose cities became major centres of scholarship, commerce and cultural exchange.
nodes.description: The Abbasid revolution established a new caliphal dynasty in 750 and shifted the political centre toward Baghdad, founded in 762. Abbasid-era networks brought scholars, translators and practitioners into contact across languages and regions. Intellectual life drew on Greek, Persian, Indian and other traditions, while political authority changed over time.

nodes.title: Ottoman Empire
nodes.short: A multiethnic empire connecting southeastern Europe, West Asia and North Africa for more than six centuries.
nodes.description: The Ottoman state emerged in Anatolia around the turn of the fourteenth century and expanded across parts of Europe, Asia and Africa. The conquest of Constantinople in 1453 made the city an imperial capital, while Ottoman institutions, law, architecture and trade shaped a broad region.

nodes.title: Safavid Dynasty
nodes.short: An Iranian dynasty that fostered a distinctive Persianate culture and state tradition.
nodes.description: The Safavid dynasty unified much of Iran in the early sixteenth century and made Twelver Shi'a Islam the state religion. Its rulers patronised architecture, painting, carpets and courtly arts, especially under Shah Abbas I. Safavid Iran interacted and competed with the Ottoman and Mughal empires.

nodes.title: Maya Civilisation
nodes.short: A diverse and living Mesoamerican civilisation known for writing, architecture, mathematics and astronomy.
nodes.description: Maya societies developed across Mesoamerica over many centuries, building city-states, monumental architecture and sophisticated systems of writing and timekeeping. Political power was distributed among multiple centres rather than a single unified empire. Maya peoples and languages remain vibrant today.

nodes.title: Mexica (Aztec) Empire
nodes.short: A powerful Mesoamerican alliance centred on Tenochtitlan and sustained by tribute and trade.
nodes.description: The Mexica-led Triple Alliance emerged in the fifteenth century and built an expansive political system centred on Tenochtitlan. Its power relied on military campaigns, tribute obligations and alliances with other city-states. The empire was defeated by Spanish-led forces and Indigenous allies in 1521.

nodes.title: Inca Empire
nodes.short: The largest empire in pre-Columbian America, organised across the Andes through roads and labour systems.
nodes.description: The Inca Empire, known in Quechua as Tawantinsuyu, expanded rapidly from its Andean heartland during the fifteenth century. Its rulers connected diverse peoples through roads, administrative centres, state storehouses and labour obligations. Inca engineering adapted to mountain environments while local communities retained distinct identities.

nodes.title: Wari Civilisation
nodes.short: An influential Andean society whose political and artistic innovations preceded Inca expansion.
nodes.description: The Wari developed in the central Andes and established a far-reaching political and cultural presence between roughly 600 and 1000 CE. Their settlements, road systems, textiles and ritual art reveal a complex society with strong regional influence. Wari and Tiwanaku were distinct formations that helped shape later Andean societies.

nodes.title: Maya Mathematics and Calendars
nodes.short: Maya mathematical and astronomical systems supported complex calendars and the recording of historical time.
nodes.description: Maya scholars developed a vigesimal, or base-twenty, numerical system and used a symbol for zero. Their calendar systems combined cycles of different lengths, while astronomical observations supported the prediction and recording of celestial events. These systems were developed within specific cultural and ceremonial contexts.

nodes.title: Indian Numerals and Global Mathematical Exchange
nodes.short: A history of mathematical ideas moving between India, the Islamic world and Europe.
nodes.description: Indian mathematical traditions developed place-value notation and the use of zero, which travelled through scholarly and commercial networks. Translations and adaptations in the Abbasid-era intellectual world helped transmit Indian numerical methods into Arabic-language scholarship and later into Europe. This was a history of exchange and transformation.

nodes.title: Ile-Ife and Yoruba Art
nodes.short: A major Yoruba urban and artistic centre renowned for naturalistic terracotta and metal sculpture.
nodes.description: Ile-Ife became an important Yoruba urban and religious centre in what is now southwestern Nigeria. Artists created accomplished terracotta and metal sculptures, including works made using lost-wax casting. Archaeological and art-historical evidence establishes the local African origins of these traditions.

nodes.title: The Shahnameh and Persian Epic Tradition
nodes.short: Ferdowsi's epic poem helped preserve and reshape pre-Islamic Iranian stories in New Persian.
nodes.description: The Shahnameh, completed by Ferdowsi around the beginning of the eleventh century, is a major epic of Persian literature. It brings together legendary and historical narratives about Iranian kings and heroes, drawing on older traditions while giving them a lasting literary form in New Persian. Manuscript production later made it central to Persian book arts.

nodes.title: Science and Translation in the Abbasid World
nodes.short: A multilingual intellectual environment where scholars translated, debated and extended knowledge from several traditions.
nodes.description: Scientific work in Abbasid-era cities involved translation, commentary, observation and original research. Scholars worked with Greek, Persian and Indian materials in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy. This movement was not confined to Baghdad or to one religious community, and knowledge circulated through wider Afro-Eurasian networks.
